items.body: Neram Pularumbol (“As The Dawn Breaks”) finds Sunken Cages pulling the rhythmic traditions of South India into an electronic vocabulary of bass, drones, and fractured club music. The album opens in celebratory, ebullient mode with “Kerala”, before “Elephant Dance” raises the tempo and “Idakka” takes a more synthetic path, processing patterns from the traditional hourglass-shaped Kerala drum. Breath soon becomes almost as important as rhythm. On “Darantee”, featuring Kuza, vocal exhalations and percussion give the music a physicality that draws on the agricultural and folk roots of South India. The connection with Kerala runs throughout the record, particularly through the collective force of its percussion traditions. “Drum and Flowers” imagines Chenda drums within a celebratory night dance, their increasingly animated rhythms rubbing against darker industrial sounds. “Athiraavile” — Malayalam for “early in the morning” or “at the break of dawn” — shifts the scene towards daybreak, combining an unprocessed Chenda melam pattern with heavy electronic beats and Rani Jambak’s incantatory voice. Throughout, traditional instruments remain clearly audible even as their rhythmic properties are stretched, fragmented and repositioned. The second half effectively takes that process apart again through a substantial series of remixes. “Drum and Flowers” alone appears in three new iterations: Weldroid, Lila Tirando a Violeta and El Kontessa pull its rhythmic framework in sharply different directions, at points veering towards acid, jungle and deconstructed club music. The source material consequently keeps changing hands and contexts, with each version exposing possibilities latent in the original. For all its electronic density, Neram Pularumbol eventually circles back towards the physical act of playing. “Kerala (Moki McFly Remix)” brings proceedings to an apt conclusion, returning percussion to a more tactile foreground and introducing distinctly jazzy, free-form leanings. The album begins and ends with “Kerala”, but the intervening transformations ensure that the return doesn’t feel quite like arriving at the same place. photo by Mike Vanemon To find out more about the production process for the album, we got in touch directly with Ravish Momin (aka Sunken Cages). The liner notes to Neram Pularumbol use resynthesis not simply as an electronic process but as a metaphor for taking culture apart into its constituent elements and putting it together differently, in opposition to the idea of tradition as something “frozen, solidified and sanctified”. That does seem particularly audible on Neram Pularumbol, where South Indian instruments and rhythmic languages are present but rarely allowed to function as straightforward markers of heritage. What exactly are you trying to preserve when you dismantle and reconstruct a tradition in this way, and at what point does transformation become more important than recognisability? Does this also connect with what you have described elsewhere as “resynthesizing the traditional” and decolonising conventional ideas of so-called global music? Thanks for this great question! The best analogy to start with is to think of making a photocopy of a photocopy. Even 8-10 generations of copies later, they do not resemble the original, get distorted and warped, and perhaps even a new narrative emerges. This process itself is of deep interest to me and what I’m hoping to preserve. When I think of a rhythm I’ve learned in the past, it’s more about how I’m recalling it in the moment, with all the unconscious inspirations and changes that get added over time- to be left with a transformation that’s an impression, an organic reimagining- similar to what happens to our own memories over time. Furthermore, I’m taking these ‘resynthesized patterns’ and placing them in a new framework of synths, drones, and other electronic elements that I’ve absorbed, to create a new global-music that simply doesn’t rely on invoking the past. I need to be careful to add that all this does not mean a blatant disrespect of the culture and tradition, but to be left with recognizable elements-like the sounds and basic structure of a pattern- in an arrangement that may be unfamiliar. That’s where the decolonizing takes shape. Music is predicated on a dynamic process of growth and evolution, yet too often non-western artists are expected to be performative of their culture, and their use of contemporary technologies or drawing inspirations from western genres is considered disingenuous. Gatekeeping and branding from western ethnomusicologists and curators has a long problematic history, but I’ll leave that discussion for another time Neram Pularumbol is particularly rooted in the musical traditions of Kerala, from the title itself to “Idakka”, named after the hourglass-shaped drum associated with Kerala’s temple music. Yet you don’t present these traditions ethnographically or attempt to reproduce them faithfully: their rhythmic and timbral characteristics are broken apart and absorbed into electronics, bass and club structures. Which particular Kerala musical traditions, instruments or rhythmic practices fed into this album, and what is your own relationship to them? Are there elements that you consciously wanted to retain in recognisable form, and others that you felt could only remain alive by being transformed? Hopefully my previous response lends some insight to this question as well. To elaborate, I’ve always found group drumming to be powerful, an action of resistance and solidarity as well as of spiritual significance. Particularly, I was mesmerized by music performances known as Chenda melam in which hundreds of artists sync and perform together during temple festivals in Kerala. The drums native to Kerala, like the Chenda, Idakka and Elathalam, also have markedly different timbres/sonorities from the North-Indian drums such as Tabla and Dhol to which one may be accustomed to hearing. While I’m originally from South India (Hyderabad) myself, I currently split my time between Brooklyn and Philadelphia. I did not grow up in Kerala, India, but I wanted to think about what a meaningful recreation of those rituals into my own worldview, that was culturally respectful as well, would represent. For example, On “Drum and Flowers,” I created a narrative with shifting tempos where the Chenda drum is used in a celebratory night dance, after the workers have come home. A multitude of drums lead the celebrations, shedding industrial grime for synchronized movements that quicken, a shared bodily memory of ancestral resistance and resilience. The song is punctuated with industrial textures and dark synth stabs that represent the rigor of factory-work. “Idakka,” the track to which you’d alluded earlier, runs the Idakka drum patterns through various delays and echo filters to create this cavernous rhythmic feel where machine-like sounds are also ever-present. Here the traditional elements are drastically transformed and chopped up, signifying a not-too-distant future where machines threaten to take over humanity. On “Athiraavile,” which features the Indonesian producer/vocalist Rani Jambak, I actually used a clean / unprocessed Chenda melam pattern on top of heavy electronic beats. Here, Rani lends a shaman-like call to prayer- not belonging to any specific religious denomination- where people gather to play drums at dawn. The second half of the album effectively allows other artists to take your rhythmic material apart again. “Drum and Flowers” is especially revealing because Weldroid, Lila Tirando a Violeta and El Kontessa pull the same source towards very different rhythmic and electronic environments, while Masma Dream World and Moki McFly produce two strikingly different versions of “Kerala” and Kush Arora makes “Idakka” considerably harsher and more propulsive. You have said that these collaborators were chosen partly through relationships you have built with artists around the world who approach tradition as something mutable rather than fixed. When you heard the finished remixes, did any of them reveal something in your own compositions that you hadn’t realised was there? And does handing the music over to artists from such different cultural and musical contexts become another stage of the album’s idea of resynthesis? The remixes were as much a part of the album as the tracks. And a resounding yes to your observation of having these remixes represent a further reshaping of the source-material, as multiple layers of resynthesis now exist Each artist brought their respective cultural background, musical aesthetic and production style to the table. Back during the pandemic lockdown in 2020, I’d actively sought out remote collaborations with artists in different corners of the globe. I do want to emphasize that it was also important for me to support women artists, do my part to highlight them in a male-dominated electronic music scene. Over the years, I’ve maintained my goal of building a musical community with diverse collaborators who all take musical risks and blend the traditional to the digital in their own practice. As an artist with a remix track-record of my own (Babani Sound System, Batida’s Ikoqwe, Depeche Mode, dragonchild and Thollem), I’ve spent a lot of time listening to a given track to quickly hone in on elements that resonated with my aesthetic- whether it was a vocal phrase, a melody or a rhythmic motif. The objective was to take apart the original track and re-stitch it back together highlighting that chosen element, in ways that wouldn’t be predictable. El Kontessa added a doumbek pattern to the underlying rhythm and made it feel like it was always there, as if South Indian and Egyptian musicians jammed all the time. Masma Dream World took the drone elements of “Kerala” which I’d intentionally layered heavily, to create a very cinematic track with a stripped down minimal beat. Weldroid’s acid synths and bit-crushed elements gave the track a dance music of the future energy. Lila Tirando a Violeta removed my rhythmic elements entirely and energized the track with a Jungle vibe. Moki Mc Fly seemed to instinctively grasp my AACM past- which was grounded in their ancient to the future motto- and brought an acoustic Free-Jazz tribute to the Art Ensemble of Chicago to his remix. Neram Pularumbol means “As The Dawn Breaks”, while the name Sunken Cages itself has a much darker environmental origin: you have described the “sunken cage” as an image of something once held captive becoming submerged by rising waters, reflecting your background in environmental engineering and longstanding concern with climate change. Yet this record often feels less apocalyptic than that image suggests: despite the drones, industrial textures and moments of considerable darkness, there is movement, colour and a sense of emergence. What does “dawn” mean within this record? Is it intended as a counterweight to the darker implications of Sunken Cages, or do you see destruction, transformation and renewal as parts of the same process? For the past few years, I’ve been thinking a lot about the duality of the nature of water, as a source of survival and also as one of destruction. While there is a sense of hopelessness that comes from realizing that some of the impacts of climate-change are irreversible, there is also hope in focussing on environmentally sustainable practices. Rather than thinking of dawn as a counterweight to the bleakness of the overarching climate narrative, I wanted to leave its symbolism ambiguous. In other words, we can meet the dawn feeling powerless or prepare to transform our future for preservation. On a broader level, the choice still doesn’t seem to have been made. As far as the tracks go, I play with the tension between the forces of darkness and rejuvenation- with the industrial sounds/textures on the verge of overpowering the ancient rhythms and chants, which signify our humanity, and certainly different tracks allude to different outcomes of that struggle. PS. Since this interview took place, Momin has released Morning Birds and Distant Drums, a new album with Haitian “soundchemist” Val Jeanty as Turning Jewels Into Water. Taking the AACM credo “Ancient to the Future” as a guiding principle, the record brings their Indian and Haitian lineages into a kinetic dialogue with improvisation and contemporary electronics. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters发行，是德国-肯尼亚鼓手Sven Kacirek与Olith Ratengo（Odd Okoddo二人组）首次同时与83岁传统肯尼亚歌手Ogoya Nengo合作的成果。Nengo来自肯尼亚东部，其多萝（Dodo）传统歌唱贯穿全片，而Ratengo与她相邻而居，使二人声部之间的呼应带有真实的血缘与文化根基。Kacirek以Buchla合成器、手打击乐与套鼓构建节奏底层，层层递进的合成复节奏（如《Bara》中由单调节拍渐次生长为有机的整体）在不淹没人声的前提下悄然浮现。《Sarah》则展示了合成器失真对Ratengo人声张力的精准刺入。文章将此类音乐置于全球语境中讨论——与Chouk Bwa、The Ångströmers及Nyege Nyege厂牌的探索性计划并置，指出当代非洲及其离散社群音乐如何在保留传统的同时以前卫姿态回应跨文化交流，使根源听起来既古老又先锋。

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Is CARDIACS a progressive rock band? The question, which may have sparked debate at one time, seems obsolete today. All we can say is that singer and guitarist Tim Smith?the band's longtime leader, its heart, mind, and soul, and now more than ever regarded as an exceptional English artist, more than five years after his passing?is a child of the vibrant prog universe that truly lives up to its name. He himself cited among his countless influences such legendary names as Genesis, Faust, Can, Gong, Zappa, and Gentle Giant?a fact confirmed by the album *A Little Man And A House And The Whole World Window*.From the very introduction of the excellent new version of the track "A Little Man and a House," it becomes clear that this album will be on an entirely different level than *Seaside*, their previous album released in 1983. The compositions date back to the previous three years, but the production is much richer than on *Seaside* and in no way tainted by the typical sound of the '80s. Musically, it's a true leap forward, with arrangements of unprecedented richness ("The Icing on the World"), sometimes bordering on unnecessary excess ("The Breakfast Line," saved by its impressive grand finale). The significant contribution of William D. Drake's keyboards (who joined the band in late 1983) is no small part of this, as the musician displays a boundless imagination that rivals Tim's. Drake also co-wrote two of the album's most progressive tracks: "I'm Eating in Bed," which appears as a bonus track?a surreal little nursery rhyme that could easily have fit on *Nursery Cryme* or *Foxtrot*; and "The Whole World Window," which closes the album in a rather unexpected way, bringing CARDIACS closer to King Crimson's *In The Court* with heavy use of mellotron, piano, and bombastic organ, thereby convincing us once and for all that this is one of the most important prog works of 1988.
items._cn_summary: 这张1988年的专辑是乐队从早期作品的一次重要飞跃，制作远比上一张专辑丰富，未沾染八十年代典型音色。编曲呈现出前所未有的层次密度，部分曲目在丰富性与过度堆砌之间游走，但整体以键盘手William D. Drake加入后带来的想象力为重要支柱。其键盘演奏与Tim Smith的创作并驾齐驱，两人共同创作的两首曲目尤为突出：前者像一首超现实的童谣，风格贴近Genesis早期作品；后者作为专辑终曲大量运用mellotron、钢琴与宏大管风琴，将乐队拉近King Crimson的领域。专辑融合了Genesis、Faust、Can、Gong、Zappa、Gentle Giant等多重影响，是该年前卫摇滚领域不可忽视的作品。

items.album: Lana Del Rabies Explores Desire and Self-Erasure in Ghostly Video for “Annihilate”
items.excerpt: An ache moves forward He steps back I step forward It all turns black He steps forward I step back Some relationships develop their own terrible choreography: one person advances, the other retreats, and a moment of contact sends both back through the same steps. On Annihilate, underground post-industrial producer and vocalist Lana Del Rabies gives that exhausted dance a setting of metallic percussion, dissonant strings, and voices that seem to drift through the walls. The prospect of closeness
items.body: An ache moves forward He steps back I step forward It all turns black He steps forward I step back Some relationships develop their own terrible choreography: one person advances, the other retreats, and a moment of contact sends both back through the same steps. On Annihilate, underground post-industrial producer and vocalist Lana Del Rabies gives that exhausted dance a setting of metallic percussion, dissonant strings, and voices that seem to drift through the walls. The prospect of closeness carries a threat of disappearance, as though reaching for another person might cost you the outline of yourself. Released through her own Feral Crone Recordings, the single revisits the gothic industrial territory of her 2023 album STREGA BEATA. Among her most accessible recordings to date, Annihilate brings its melody into clearer view within a dense, unsettling arrangement, with echoes of mid-career Nine Inch Nails, early Chelsea Wolfe, Dead Can Dance, and Godflesh. Written and produced by Lana Del Rabies, the track features bass, guitar, and additional instrumentation from Zach Wise, formerly of experimental black metal band Hissing. Deeply reverberant string tones open the song, their discord setting the room askew before a soft metallic beat begins carrying it forward. Creaking noises punctuate the haze, while thudding distortion stays buried beneath the mix, suggesting a heartbeat accelerating at the approach of something unwelcome. Her singing is soft, breathy, and eerily close; farther away, wails stretch across the recording like cries attempting to reach the living. The whole thing suggests a deserted Victorian factory, its decaying rooms still occupied by machinery and something considerably harder to identify. That dusty, corroded atmosphere recalls the gothic industrial aesthetics of the 1990s, with every small sound acquiring an uncomfortable physical presence. The lyrics begin with images converging in reverse and a moment suspended in time. From there, the exchange becomes a sequence of opposing movements: his withdrawal prompts her advance, his approach sends her backward. “Push pull fade” reduces the relationship to its recurring mechanism. Hearing her name briefly promises recognition, but the next attempt at contact leaves her grasping in vain. By the time the title enters the refrain, desire reads as a force capable of wearing away the person who feels it. Directed and edited by Lana Del Rabies/Sam An, the video translates that instability into grainy woodland footage, overlapping figures, and close-ups that dissolve before they can offer much certainty. Pale dresses and fabric catch the light against dense foliage; raised arms, blurred faces, and bodies close to the ground recur through successive layers of exposure. Black-and-white images give way to smeared color, turning the setting into something resembling a damaged reel of folk horror. The footage was shot by Jane Slater, whose video credits include Dildox, Brood Faye, and Sacred Skin, and Vox Porter of Sleek Teeth. Watch the video for Annihilate below: Lana Del Rabies began with early experiments sampling female pop musicians into noise tracks, a practice reflected in the project’s name. An has since developed a body of work spanning industrial music, gothic electronics, and experimental heaviness, examining human brutality and the prospect of apocalypse. Her recordings have earned attention from The Quietus, Metal Hammer, and Anthony Fantano, while her live performances have taken her to festivals including Roadburn, Coldwaves, Sled Island, Prepare the Ground, Northwest Terror Fest, and Soulcrusher. She has toured with Author & Punisher, 3TEETH, Pharmakon, JPEGMAFIA, and John Wiese, and opened shows for artists including clipping., Midwife, HEALTH, and Bell Witch. In 2025, An founded the art-focused label Feral Crone Recordings and released Le Temps Viendra and Omnipotent Fuck. She is currently working on a studio record with former members of Hissing, due in 2027. Listen to Annihilate below and order the single here. Annihilate by Lana Del Rabies Lana Del Rabies joins gothic rock vocalist Echos for a West Coast tour this October. items._cn_summary: Lana Del Rabies以独立厂牌Feral Crone Recordings发行单曲《Annihilate》，延续其2023年专辑STREGA BEATA的哥特工业路线。曲目以深邃回响的弦乐开启，不和谐的音调令空间扭曲，金属打击乐推进节拍，失真低频隐于混音之下，暗示心跳在某种不安逼近时加速。嗓音轻柔、呼吸感强烈，远处则伸展着如泣般的哀号，整体声场营造出废弃维多利亚工厂的腐朽氛围。歌词以"推拉消退"概括亲密关系中的反复机制，将欲望描绘为足以消磨主体自我的力量。编曲借鉴九寸钉、Chelsea Wolfe、Dead Can Dance与Godflesh的气质，旋律在密集不安的编排中反而获得更清晰的呈现。音乐录像以林间颗粒影像与多重曝光展开，黑白画面逐渐化为污损的彩色胶片，呈现出民谣恐怖片式的损伤质感，将歌词中关系的脆弱与不稳定转化为视觉语言。

items.body: This album from the Danish project Black Vault was actually released quite some time ago—back in the spring of 2025. With the telling title “Death Obsessed”, we are presented with five tracks. There is no room for fun in this sonic universe; instead, we are confronted with a dark, nihilistic-sounding whole. The atmosphere is carefully constructed and accentuated by occasional spoken-word samples, creating a tormented listening experience. Blending elements of Dark-Ambient, Industrial, Noise, and even Ritual music, the production is sometimes a tiny chaotic yet undeniably well-crafted. The combination of influences is fascinating, and, to my mind, the opening two tracks are particularly compelling. Black Vault transports us into an illusory world of ruin. The only thing missing, for me, is an absolute climax—though that certainly doesn’t mean this isn’t a great record. (Rating:7½). Listen to “The Hollow Sighs Of Putrid Emission”: The Hollow Sighs Of Putrid Emission by Black Vault About Black Vault Black Vault is a Danish project working in occult industrial and death-industrial territory on the German label Dunkelheit Produktionen. The project’s debut album, “Hymns To The Great Devourer”, was released on Dunkelheit Produktionen in 2023. “Death Obsessed” is the follow-up, recorded between 2023 and 2024 and released on March 1, 2025, mixed and mastered by Grant Richardson at Hex Audio Labs.
items._cn_summary: 丹麦项目Black Vault的第二张专辑《Death Obsessed》由德国地下厂牌Dunkelheit Produktionen发行，收录五首作品。整张专辑以黑暗虚无主义为基调，融合暗氛围、工业、噪音乃至仪式音乐的多种元素，营造出被侵蚀与崩塌的听觉氛围。制作中偶尔加入口语采样来强化精神折磨感，整体编排虽偶显混乱却经得起推敲。开篇两首尤为突出，将听众拖入一个由废墟与幻象构筑的声音空间。专辑缺乏一个绝对的高潮点，但作为一张精心营造氛围的地下工业作品，其层次与质感已足够扎实。

In the same land that spawned Wayne Shorter, Sarah Vaughan and the famed Van Gelder studios, there seems to be an endless amount of artists pushing the boundaries on the genre today, from the hallucinatory prog-funk fusion of New Brunswick’s Guesstimate and Asbury Park’s We Used to Cut the Grass, to the improvisatory adventurousne
items.body: New Jersey’s multifaceted world of underground music features a healthy amount of experimental jazz, mutating into various new and unique directions. In the same land that spawned Wayne Shorter, Sarah Vaughan and the famed Van Gelder studios, there seems to be an endless amount of artists pushing the boundaries on the genre today, from the hallucinatory prog-funk fusion of New Brunswick’s Guesstimate and Asbury Park’s We Used to Cut the Grass, to the improvisatory adventurousness of Paterson’s Thieves in Paris. Yet one name that always seems to appear while discussing the current state of Jersey jazz, and that is Mike Noordzy. From projects like El Noordzo, Mothguts and the Mike Noordzy Quintet, the Middlesex County-dwelling multi-instrumentalist never ceases to wow and amaze with his genre-defying sounds and unorthodox approaches. One of my favorite of his many albums was the shadowy avant-jazz soundscape that is Shark Funeral Songbook, released under his Noordzo moniker back in 2017. Nearly ten years later, he’s released a follow up, Shark Funeral Songbook Vol. 2, and it defied the odds and outshines the original. The album squirms and throbs with murky life, as it swings from percussion and string-based tracks that echo the works of Moondog, to surreal noir drifts and cataclysmic jazz-metal sludge and beyond. The album is a deep and varied collage of all kinds of styles and flavors, often blending and clashing together within a single track. The end result may offer hints of the likes of Tom Waits, Peter Brötzmann and, in the case of the harder tracks, Noordzy’s own Mothguts project, yet there is really no other album quite like this one. Between the collision of disparate genres, greasy textures, gritty atmospherics and unhinged rhythms all bleeding together within a very musique concrète-styled mix, this is a truly one-of-a-kind musical experience. The more you listen to this spooky record, the more you get pulled into its vastly immersive sonic world, and the more you feel like you’re getting a glimpse into the busy mind of a multifaceted artist who can channel their creativity into a thousand different directions at a moment’s notice. Boundless, unpredicatble and endlessly entertaining, Shark Funeral Songbook vol. 2 is a must have for fans of Sonny Sharrock, Colin Stetson and Moor Mother. Click here to get your copy today for Bandcamp Friday! -KH
items._genre: avant-garde jazz / experimental / fusion / noir / improvisation
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是新泽西地下音乐人 Mike Noordzy 在《Shark Funeral Songbook》七年后的续作，延续并超越了原作的暗黑前卫爵士气质。整张作品呈现出碎片化的拼贴结构，在单一曲目内不断碰撞、撕裂并重组爵士、噪音摇滚、朋克金属与具体音乐等多种风格。打击乐与弦乐驱动的段落呼应 Moondog 的街头韵律，间或滑入超现实的黑色电影式漂浮段落，又突然爆发为爵士-金属泥浆般的重型音墙。混音手法深受 musique concrète 影响，肮脏的质感与颗粒感十足的氛围层叠交织，节奏线不羁而难以预测。专辑并非线性聆听体验，而是邀请听者反复潜入其沉浸式声场，逐步揭开创作者繁复而多向的创意脉络。

items.tags: クラシック 現代音楽 intoxicate 2026 August クラシック 現代音楽 # リイシュー クラシック 里見暁美 松平頼暁
items.excerpt: 『ピアノ・ホライズン』に80年代の日本の音楽シーンを垣間見る。ローズからモールス信号のような単音の連打が聴こえ、クラヴィのクラスターが連打を断ち切る。ファンキーな音色にマイルス・デイヴィスの音楽のようだと感じるが、リズムにグルーヴが感じられるわけではない。松平頼暁がこのアルバムを企画したピアニスト里見暁美に書き下ろした“エリクサトーン”だ。しばらくしてピアノが緩やかに辿る下降音形が聴こえ、そこに時折りピアノからの異音が混じり、雨後のアスファルトから昇る蒸気のような音場が立ち上がる。藤枝守の“フォーリング・スケール第6番”だ。この二人の作品は〈表現内容よりも構造が強調〉されていると近藤譲はノートに記す。

items._cn_summary: 这张1981年发行的专辑由日本钢琴家里見暁美演绎，呈现了两位作曲家松平頼暁与藤枝守的现代钢琴作品。松平頼暁的《エリクサトーン》以单音连打开场，电钢琴音色呈现类似funk的质感，却缺乏爵士的律动，更接近结构化的实验声响。藤枝守的《フォーリング・スケール第6番》则以缓慢的下降音形展开，偶发的钢琴异音营造出雨后沥青蒸腾般的声场。乐评引用近藤譲的笔记，指出这两部作品的核心特征在于结构的优先性而非表现内容。专辑为听众提供了80年代日本当代古典音乐创作中结构主义倾向的一个窗口。

items.body: When John Coltrane died in 1967 the jazz world felt a startling void. With the release of Expression , Coltrane’s final studio album, it must have felt like a narrative had been cut short of its intended ending. After all, unless Trane had recorded material that had never been released, that was it: no more new music from John Coltrane. We know the story 100 years after Trane’s birth, however. And did he ever record material that had yet to be released! Alice Coltrane worked relentlessly to preserve John’s towering musical legacy, and we know from Andy Beta’s incisive book on her life that after a long day of raising four children on her own, she would put the kids to bed, sit in meditation, and practice the music that meant so much to her and her late husband. What she also did was listen to unreleased recordings by John and prepare them for release. Among the recordings made public in the immediate years following John’s passing were two absolutely stunning (I can’t emphasize this word enough– stunning! ) recordings by the famed Classic Quartet of Trane, McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones: Transition in 1970 and Sun Ship in 1971. Transition McCoy Tyner related to writer David Wild that sometimes John would give them two notes, or maybe just a scale, as the basis of a composition before they recorded. The title track to the album Transition, recorded in the spring of 1965 , certainly could be such a piece. The work features a tightly focused quartet that absolutely opens up the gates and begins to tear down the fences. “Transition” is one the group’s wildest, most ferociously open pieces. It’s as though the catalytic power of Ascension or Om has been concentrated into a narrow and controlled conduit. Both the kinetic energy coursing through that conduit and the narrowness of the channel itself create the conditions for tension and combustion. The “Prayer and Meditation Suite,” on the other hand, is an absolute masterwork. I am of the persuasion that comparing works of Trane to other periods in his life can dangerously undervalue some of his accomplishments. Any suite, be it Meditations or “Prayer and Meditation” would beg comparison with A Love Supreme . Forget all that. “Prayer and Meditation” would stand as one the great works in the jazz canon if it were the only piece Coltrane and the Quartet created. Movement II: “Peace and After” is the sound of a quest for peace complete with all the pain inherent in that search. Movement IV: “Affirmation” picks up where “Transition” left off and rings with crisis, explosiveness, and spiritual urgency. Violence was always slinking nearby during Coltrane’s life, as it is for us today, and his music embraces this reality, but I would never describe his music as “violent.” Just note the third remaining song on Transition : “Dear Lord.” It is hard for me to imagine there ever existed a world without this vulnerable dedication to peace. Urgency and catharsis. Peace and vulnerability. The circumstances without and the transition within. Sun Ship In the nighttime hours of August 26, 1965, John Coltrane and his classic quartet walked into an East Manhattan studio. That year Martin Luther King and hundreds of peaceful protestors were arrested in Selma for wanting voter registration fairness. Malcolm X was shot to death. The first massive contingent of US ground troops landed in Vietnam, and the United States would slaughter tens of thousands of people before the year ended using machine guns and missiles fired from military jets. In Los Angeles, unemployment rates for black Americans grew to levels greater than during the Great Depression, housing discrimination was bolstered by law, and Watts exploded in rioting after a violent encounter between police and a black man. John Coltrane placed his mouth around his horn and blew. The sound that emerged, a passage of lyrical melody deeply tender and filled with solace, titled “Dearly Beloved,” lifted into the air. John embodied serenity and the path to it. People were dying and being denied their humanity by a power structure that required their destruction, and John never pretended this was not the case. The path to peace traveled through pain, not around it. People are dying right now as you read this, but life’s powerful play goes on, in all of its tragedy and real joy. Afterall, John’s baby boy Ravi had just been born, and John had assembled this collection of musicians to record at night because that day he was busy celebrating his first son, John Jr. 's, first birthday. Attaining does not come without suffering, but it also arrives with beauty. Attaining. Sun Ship. Ascent. Amen. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: free jazz / avant-garde / spiritual jazz / post-bop
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了Coltrane经典四重奏1965年春录制的两张专辑《Transition》（1970年发行）与《Sun Ship》（1971年发行），属于他生前未曾正式发表的遗作。评论指出，Coltrane有时仅给乐手两个音或一个音阶作为即兴创作的基础，《Transition》同名曲正是这种极端自由创作理念的体现——四重奏在狭窄的通道中汇聚出强烈的动能张力与爆发力。《Prayer and Meditation Suite》被评论视为独立于《A Love Supreme》之外依然成立的杰作，其第二乐章'Peace and After'承载了对和平的痛苦追寻，第四乐章'Affirmation'延续了前曲的精神紧迫感。整张合辑呈现出自由爵士后期的极致能量、精神性与不可控的创造力，是Coltrane遗产中由Alice Coltrane整理保存并最终公开的重要文献。

items.body: Felice Sciorilli first graced our pages last spring, appearing on Biodiversità Records’ 14 Soundcapes with the track “Breaths.” At the time, we recognized the unique nature of the piece, capturing the sound of “air pushed through the Etruscan sandstone cliffs by the incoming waves.” “Breaths” appears on Distant Places as well, a worthy inclusion. In a way, the album title is a misnomer. These places are not necessarily geographically distant; most come from the intertidal zone of the Tyrrhenian Sea. But as Sciorilli has a particular fascination with tide pools – some only centimeters deep – these sounds may be regarded as distant as most people seldom if ever encounter their nuances. When one hears that an album is recorded at the coast, one expects to hear a bevy of predictable material: wind and waves, gulls and other fair-weather fowls. These make appearances, but are not primary. Instead, Sciorilli concentrates on micro-sounds made macro. In “E,” water rushes into crevasses before spurting back out, powered by the force of the waves, although this is not technically the sound of the waves. Instead, this is the sound of waves in rocks, familiar to jetty walkers. As the angles of approach vary, so do the timbres. The tide pools first come into focus in the opening segment of “Cluster,” with a sound akin to the crackle of brine shrimp. The piece develops in movements, like the “Bohemian Rhapsody” of field recording. Soon there are crashing waves, then fizzes and pops, and finally the sound of pebbles tossing, turning, rolling back to the sea. “Bolle” and “Bubbles drift upward into the water” occupy different areas of the album while also being separated by tone. While hearing them, one recalls pablo diserens’ “The Shrinking Glacier” from last year’s ebbing ice lines, providing one with the opportunity to compare “healthy” bubbles with “unhealthy” bubbles, or bubbles that belong to a cycle with those escaping for the last time. The second piece is more effervescent, like alien birds swimming in soda; without hydrophones, one might never encounter such distant sounds. While listening, one is amazed by the number of musical parallels that can be found in nature: the quickening tempos of “From the Tidal Edge,” the glissandos of “Outflow.” Distant Places serves as a reminder that music imitates nature, not (save for starlings) the other way around. The set builds to the eighteen-minute centerpiece “Tiny Worlds,” a longer, reworked version of a piece that made the shortlist of The Radiophonic Broadcast’s Sounds of the Year 2025-26. Recorded in a tidal pool six centimeters deep (shown in the pdf that accompanies the download), the piece demonstrates just how rich, dense and diverse a micro-world can be, although to be fair, to the local Littorina snails there also exist micro-worlds within micro-worlds, from bacteria down to the smallest atom, each with a corresponding biophony. The “characters” that appear may be animate or inanimate, but each possesses a personality of its own: squeaking and whistling, popping and percolating. In the final piece, Sciorilli draws back from the water and embeds his microphone in the sand, muffling the sound of the nearby waves. “Under the Sand” operates as a parable. Sonic treasures are available everywhere, yet most of us never hear them; it is as if we too are buried in the sand, listening through wax and debris, treating micro-worlds as distant places although they are right beneath our feet. (Richard Allen)
items._genre: field recording / sound art / electroacoustic / ambient
items._cn_summary: 这是一张以田野录音为核心的声音艺术专辑，作者将录制设备贴近地中海潮间带的微小缝隙与潮池，捕捉水流入岩缝喷射而出、卤虫噼啪作响、碎石翻滚回海等宏观化处理的微声。专辑虽然名为《远方之地》，但所指并非地理距离，而是大多数听众极少留意的声音细部。作品结构类似多乐章套曲，从水流的节奏与音高变化，到气泡上升的层次差异，再到长达十八分钟的潮池中心曲，逐层揭示微型声学世界的密度与多样性。评论特别提到与冰川退缩录音的比较，赋予这些声音环境议题的隐喻。整体呈现一种将自然声响当作可被聆听、可被类比为音乐的创作观念，强调感知方式的拓展而非旋律本身。

items.body: Review by Logan — There is a distinct emotional friction at the core of Music Has the Right to Children. The album triggers a sense of nostalgia in me, but it rarely feels entirely safe or comforting. Instead, my own experience with the record lands in a bittersweet, somewhat haunted territory where the degraded educational samples and childhood imagery evoke memories that feel slightly wrong or displaced. When I listen to it, the music operates rather like a half-forgotten television broadcast from my youth left to rot on a discarded VHS tape.A significant reason this atmosphere connects with me is the physical groove of the record. Unlike the colder, more mechanical programming of their later electronic peers, the rhythm section here strikes me as dusty and organic. My personal standout of this approach is "Aquarius". The track anchors its counting-game vocal samples with a heavy, driving bassline and a hip-hop breakbeat that commands the room. To me, it represents a clear instance of the duo's ability to blend a functional rhythmic pocket with an unsettling psychological undertone.That rhythmic focus carries right through what I consider the rest of the album's essential highlights. The deliberate, motorik propulsion of "Happy Cycling" provides a steady late-album surge, while the texturally complex beat on "An Eagle in Your Mind" showcases their approach to analog tape manipulation. Even on a short, melodic pop vignette like "Roygbiv", which could easily slide into saccharine territory, I find that the underlying groove ensures the track does not dissolve into pure sentimentality. The brothers keep the project grounded in a heavy, physical reality that I find myself returning to.The technical production of the album indicates that this texture was not accidental. The Sandison brothers achieved this frayed quality through a process of analog degradation, treating their studio like a laboratory for decaying magnetic tape. Instead of relying on the digital precision of late-nineties sequencing, the duo ran their synthesizers, frequently utilising the warm, unstable sub-bass of the Roland SH-101 and the gritty digital-to-analog character of the Ensoniq VFX-SD, directly into decrepit tape machines. By bouncing audio onto consumer-grade Tascam four-track recorders and malfunctioning Grundig decks, they subjected clean melodies to physical wow-and-flutter, artificial dropouts, and tape saturation.This production method transforms standard subtractive synthesis into a tactile experience. On tracks like "An Eagle in Your Mind", the skittering rhythm section and warped vocal elements sound to my ears as though they are actively dissolving under the friction of a sticking tape head. Similarly, the low-end thunk and swirling synths of "Aquarius" owe their presence to low bit-depth Akai S1000 samplers, which naturally crush the high frequencies and add a distinctive, dusty grit to the breakbeat. By leaning into the unpredictable quirks of old gear rather than flawless digital tracks, the duo built a soundscape where everything feels beautifully decayed, matching how human memory blurs over time.This focus on unstable analog hardware explains why simpler pop tracks like "Roygbiv" still resonate with me. The track is built on a straightforward melodic hook, but the underlying production ensures it does not sound cheap or overly sweet. The bassline carries a heavy, physical thrum that balances out the drifting, sun-baked top melodies, proving to me that the duo could write an infectious pop tune without losing their signature sonic grit. It functions as my personal gateway into the album's stranger, more texturally complex spaces.By the time the record reaches "Happy Cycling", that playful energy has mutated into something far more relentless. The track acts as a steady late-album surge, driving forward on a cyclical, motorik rhythm that feels both hypnotic and slightly ominous. The repetition does not tire me out; instead, it locks me into a specific, heavy-limbed trance that mirrors the physical exhaustion of a long journey. By placing this sprawling, rhythmic marathon near the end of the tracklist, the Sandison brothers solidify the album's broader structural arc, ensuring the listener finishes the experience immersed in their strange, loop-based universe.Looking back at this debut from the vantage point of their broader discography reveals just how crucial these early structural choices were. Music Has the Right to Children acted as the foundational source code for many sonic mutations that followed across the next three decades. The warm, electro-acoustic infrastructure and acoustic guitar textures that defined The Campfire Headphase find their genetic origin here in the brief, pastoral transitions of "The Color of the Fire" and "Olson". The duo was already learning how to evoke nostalgia, laying the groundwork for a lighter, more organic detour before their mid-career pivot.The album contains the initial seeds of the cold, apocalyptic dread that eventually emerged on Tomorrow's Harvest. The unsettling vocal mutations on "An Eagle in Your Mind" and the eerie, numeric counting games of "Aquarius" are early warning signs of the claustrophobic, paranoid environments that defined their later records. By balancing infectious hip-hop grooves against a deeply haunted psychological undertone, Music Has the Right to Children did not just launch the Sandison brothers' career; it established a timeless tension that they would spend the next thirty years refining, dismantling, and rebuilding.Ultimately, Music Has the Right to Children remains a significant achievement because it refuses to age. While the late-nineties electronic scene largely chased hyper-polished digital futures, Boards of Canada looked backward, constructing a sonic monument out of decaying magnetic tape and fragmented childhood ghosts. It is a record that asks me to surrender my internal clock and sit with the discomfort of its bittersweet, haunted landscapes. Nearly three decades after its release, its physical grooves and emotional friction continue to command authority, standing for me as the definitive masterpiece of a discography that has yet to be replicated.While I do consider this album to be a masterpiece, "Aquarius" in particular remains one of my favourite Boards of Canada tracks, and this was one of my favourite albums for years. However, after getting Tomorrow's Harvest, this does not appeal to me as much. Music Has the Right to Children and Geogaddi were my favourite BoC albums, but now those final three mean more to me. So this masterpiece will get a 4 at PA (I would go with 4.5 if we had the option as I did at RYM). Additionally, I primarily wanted to add BoC to Prog Archives for the final three albums.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以童年教育录音采样与童年意象为核心，营造出苦乐交织的心理氛围。评论者特别强调节奏部分的'尘封有机'特质——区别于同期更冷峻机械的电子乐制作，专辑中的节拍给人以物理重量感。Aquarius 的嘻哈碎拍与低音线、Happy Cycling 的持续推进、An Eagle in Your Mind 的复杂节奏质感，均体现了作者对节奏肌理的关注。在制作层面，Sandison 兄弟将 Roland SH-101 合成器与 Akai 采样器直接灌入老旧卡带录音机，通过磁带物理衰减、wow-and-flutter 失真、信号丢失等手段，将原本干净的减法合成声音转化为带有触感的、仿佛在劣质磁带下溶解的物质体验。这种模拟降质技术赋予整张专辑一种半遗忘的电视广播般的怀旧感，让熟悉的童年记忆始终带有不安的底色。

items.body: I gave myself the power of keeping you away Wrapped up in the sounds of the bastion’s coldest waves I still see you watching me move towards the within Frankie Diez seems to have reached the useful stage in an artist’s life where embarrassment stops being a factor. Casual Confrontation began on indie-pop ground, but after five albums since 2020, Diez has clearly decided there are worse things than making the music you actually wanted to hear when you were younger, hanging around punk and goth scenes, absorbing whatever seeped in through the walls. “I’ve always been inspired and involved within the punk, goth, and alternative subcultures, and it’s about time my music began reflecting that,” says Diez. You can hear that decision all over SCARED OF SILENCE, the second single from Casual Confrontation’s forthcoming album BASTION. Moving deeper into darkwave and coldwave, Diez has hit upon a combination that feels absurdly overdue: reggaeton and those colder electronic forms sound like tenants who have spent years banging on opposite sides of the same wall, only to discover they were keeping time together. The guitars come in with that severe Twin Tribes economy, the bass carries some of Boy Harsher’s nightclub menace, and beneath it sits a rhythm that keeps trying to pull the song somewhere warmer, dirtier, and more physical. Reggaeton reveals repetition as pressure; a dembow rhythm can keep working on you until thought becomes secondary. EBM has spent decades using similar repetition for control, tension, intimidation, and release. Put them together and suddenly the distance between Bad Bunny and Ultra Sunn starts looking much shorter than anyone bothered to admit. By the second half, the resemblance to Karol G and Tokischa becomes harder to miss. The track loosens at the waist while retaining its colder frame, and that friction gives it personality. Ministry once made metallic percussion feel like a municipal requirement; Diez borrows some of that hard impact and drops it into a song that would rather dance than march. He has a name for the approach, too: “Reggaeton Gótico,” which sounds at first like the sort of phrase somebody invents at closing time and then regrets by breakfast. Except the music holds up the joke. Diez explains why with a much simpler answer: “I always listened to reggaeton growing up in both Puerto Rico and in Miami, and the genre fusion always felt natural, since much of reggaeton can easily have somewhat of a dark-clubbing atmosphere already.” Lyrically, SCARED OF SILENCE continues the story begun in the previous single, ARREBATO, carrying the sense of an unsafe outside world into a more private confrontation. Here, safety means shutting out the person who made the world feel threatening and looking inward for somewhere to stand. Meditative yet fierce, the song casts silence as a way to reclaim power from a toxic dynamic, finding a strange pleasure in no longer owing someone access. When an argument reaches a point where even explaining becomes exhausting, Silence becomes the final boundary, and the anger behind it settles into deliberate withdrawal. There is control in choosing when the conversation ends, especially when every earlier exchange has left someone else setting the terms. Diez gives that decision room to breathe, treating solitude as a place where the self can begin to take shape again. One lyric extends that idea across BASTION as a whole: “When the outside space no longer feels safe, I’ll leave here to see what my heart creates.” The line supplies the forthcoming album BASTION’s central premise, with retreat becoming an opportunity to make something from whatever remains beyond another person’s reach. By the end, the recurring question about silence has changed shape. It sounds almost taunting now, as if Diez already knows the answer and has finally stopped caring whether the other person admits it. items.body: This new album by Alessandro Tedeschi—better known by his sonic alter ego, Netherworld—is a remarkable work. Quite by chance, thanks to his young daughter, he stumbled upon old recordings dating back more than twenty years. These were recordings he had all but forgotten. Upon rediscovering them and realizing that their atmosphere perfectly matched the dark, sombre period he had been going through in recent months, he decided to revisit and rework material that no one had ever heard before. You could quite rightly call these Netherworld’s earliest experiments. Seven tracks were salvaged and restored. They fit seamlessly into the concept of Glacial Movements—Alessandro’s own label—leaving a profound, icy impression through their Ambient and Cinematic sound. We discover a Soundscape created—and, above all, inspired—by early expeditions to the North Pole. Distinctive field recordings echo through the metallic tones. You sense the imaginary presence of malevolent forces watching you, potentially pushing you towards a state of paranoia; you experience a sense of evil and an invisible presence that relentlessly pursues you. This effect is achieved simply through the power of the compositions, which, in my opinion, might well be hailed as Netherworld’s finest work. The sound is authentic and archaic, with deep, dominating tones that hit their mark with undeniable impact. It is hardly surprising, then, that the only track that failed to fully captivate me was the most ethereal one on the album. When music becomes an expression of dark thoughts, an artist is often at their most inspired—a fact perfectly embodied by the evocative title, “The Hermit”. (Rating:8). Listen to “Loneliness”: Loneliness by Netherworld About Netherworld Netherworld is the moniker of Alessandro Tedeschi, an Italian ambient and dark ambient composer based in Rome. The project is released through Tedeschi’s own label Glacial Movements, which he founded in 2006; “The Hermit” marks the label’s 20th anniversary. Netherworld’s music draws on manipulated fragments of classical music and field recordings, including ice masses, aurora-related material and Arctic wind recordings. Before focusing on Glacial Movements, the project released music through labels including Fario, Angle Rec, Umbra and Taalem. “Eternal Frost”, recorded in 2004, was originally issued by Umbra in a hand-numbered edition of 99 copies and later appeared on Bandcamp in February 2022. The Glacial Movements catalogue includes “Mørketid” (2007), “Over The Summit” (2011) and “Alchemy Of Ice” (2013, Tedeschi’s tenth full-length release). In 2017, Netherworld collaborated with Eraldo Bernocchi on “Himuro” for the label’s Iceberg Series. “Algida Bellezza” followed in 2019, and Side-Line’s interview with Netherworld was built around that release. “Vanishing Lands” appeared in 2022 and the Bvdub collaboration “Equilibrium” in 2023. “The Hermit” returns to material recorded before Glacial Movements existed: seven tracks salvaged from deteriorated CD-Rs and Minidiscs recorded in 2004.
items._genre: dark ambient / cinematic ambient / field recording
items._cn_summary: 意大利作曲家Alessandro Tedeschi以Netherworld之名推出的《The Hermit》，源自二十余年前偶然发现的一批早期录音作品。七首曲目经修复与重新制作后，融入其自创厂牌Glacial Movements的北极主题概念。整体声音围绕早期北极探险意象展开，冰原风声、极光质感与金属质感的环境录音交织，塑造出寒冷、孤立、带有隐隐威胁感的氛围空间。评论指出，这种深沉的压迫感与偏执情绪是通过纯粹的作曲力量达成的，而非依赖后期修饰，作品被评价为Netherworld迄今最佳。唯一未能完全打动评论者的是其中最具缥缈感的一首。作为厂牌二十周年纪念之作，该专辑回溯了Glacial Movements尚未存在时期的实验源头，将封存的声音以新的语境重新呈现给听众。

items.body: Birdsong, shifting ssshhhh, guitar string ping: rarely is it so immediately clear how the perception of things affects the perception of other things happening in the same space, in the same moment. And yet these musical events were not concurrent at the moment they were recorded to disk, even though they became so later, at the moment of playback; nor did their performers have any idea of what their collaborators would be performing. At the request of Melange Edition curator Ryoko Akama, three composers (Michael Pisaro, lo wie, and Manfred Werder) sent three scores each to three performers (Angharad Davies, Cristián Alvear, and d’incise), who picked three scores at random and recorded them without being aware of the choices made by the other performers. The three sets of three recordings were then overlaid by Akama to create three new pieces. Didn’t that string just ping in reflective response to that electronic chirp? Didn’t Alvear just pause what sounded like an attack on his guitar with a chisel to let Davies intone a group of letters, her voice cracking slightly on the last letter in anticipation of the bowl d’incise is about to drag across a stone floor? No, they couldn’t have heard one another. Their dots are scattered according to separate logics, any lines between them being drawn purely in the ear of the listener, like the alignments of aural constellations in a sky of silence. It’s as if causality is an illusion. Though the project participants all stress in the liner notes their trust in Akama, they each admit to being amazed by the quality and musicality of the outcomes, and with good reason: each track simply sounds like good music. The work is based on a willingness to throw things wide open to a range of possibilities and to trust in the senses of listeners, rather than the laws of any musical tradition or theory of harmony or melody, to sort things out. That such a strategy so often produces pleasing and enthralling results points to the ways in which our brains seem predisposed to seek and find coherence, even in the least promising of confuddlements. Similar propensities for joining the metaphorical dots have been observed experimentally in all sorts of areas, from facial recognition to language acquisition. In fact, it’s possible that the whole of consciousness itself can be attributed to these sense-making practices, these habits of turning an apparently disparate jumble of stimuli into something resembling a world. Musings on the nature of consciousness seem like quite a departure from a music project such as “3 + 3 = 3”, but the relevant point is that the correspondences and coherences that emerge across the three pieces aren’t just happy coincidences. Rather, they are signs that everything is working as it should: that composers and performers and listeners are engaged in the collaborative act of making sense of things, separated by time and space and yet entangled somehow, such that each completes the others’ thoughts. In short, all the things needed for making music are present, even if centralised control and an overarching plan in the mind of one individual are not. There’s a powerful sense of communion in this, as well as discovery.     Michael Pisaro lo wie Manfred Werder Angharad Davies Cristián Alvear d’incise Melange Edition
items._genre: experimental / contemporary classical / reductionism / sound art
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由策展人Ryoko Akama发起，邀请三位作曲家（Pisaro、lo wie、Manfred Werder）各写三份乐谱，分别交给三位演奏者（Davies、Alvear、d'incise），后者随机抽取乐谱录制，彼此互不知晓对方选择。Akama随后将三组录音叠加，创造出三首新作品。评论指出，尽管演奏者在录制时完全独立，叠加后却产生了令人信服的音乐呼应——鸟鸣、吉他泛音与人声之间仿佛存在因果关系。乐评将这种巧合归因于人类大脑天生在杂乱刺激中寻求连贯性的认知倾向，从面孔识别到语言习得均如此。这种不依赖传统和声与旋律规则、而将意义交由听众感官去构建的方式，使作品成为一次关于意识与感知本质的听觉实验。独立小厂牌发行，整体内容充足以支撑深度乐评。

items.body: BEAST (Birmingham ElectroAcoustic Sound Theatre) is a multichannel sound associated with the University of Birmingham’s Electroacoustic Music Studios,comprising of as many as 100 speakers. With these speakers encircling the audience, it’s possible to produce many spatial and acousmatic effects. What this often translates to in practice is a genre of music that leans heavily on fast, dynamic transitions between different kinds of sound and different positions in the aural field (that sphere around your head that establishes the distance up to which you can hear), and on sounds that uniformly impress when played on a multichannel sound system: bell-like sounds, rushing noise, and bass thumps, among several others. Many of my favourite pieces at BEAST FEaST 2016 eschewed this aesthetic, or rather subjected the most useful parts of it to different creative ideals. Ben Peers’ soothing, quiet drones were a welcome shift of mood from some of the more aggressive aural assaults perpetrated using the BEAST system, though the lower frequency rumble seemed added simply for the sake of acousmatic convention. In Emma Margetson’s ‘Tick’, the ticking of a metronome was shifted, splintered, and refracted in the temporal and spatial domains, with subtle pitched musical tones helping to imply the space through which the ticking moved. Annie Mahtani’s ‘Aeolian’ used quiet chords in its evocation of a quiet rainstorm and its aftermath; though her field recordings consisted of often-heard staples such as passing traffic, the magic of the piece lay in how these sounds were transformed by the dampness left by the rain (even the wind sounded different). Charlie Lockwood’s fairytale ambient musicboxes got progressively darker and grittier, before ending on an elegiac note. And Helene Hedsund’s ‘Bus No. 1’, as well as using bass to make the floor vibrate like that of a bus, also featured some nice harmonies that gradually unravelled into cacophony in a very pleasing way. Most of the above featured harmony of some sort or other, but some of the more surprising and striking pieces at the festival didn’t foreground harmony at all. I really liked Tsun Winston Yeung’s ‘Variations’, in which the composer’s EEG-measured brainwaves helped to control the sound as he meditated, read a book, did sums, and memorised text in an engaging piece of stagecraft. Another memorable performance came from Kosmas Giannoutakis, who periodically left the grand piano he was playing to walk round the circle of speakers surrounding the audience, while algorithms took the piano sounds and spun them into dense echoing textures. Luca Danieli’s ‘La Tabula Rasa’ used manipulated, machine-like spoken voice and a dose of grim humour to relate the loneliness and abjection of a web server buried deep in a network. I was probably the only person in the Elgar Concert Hall who wasn’t blown away by Jonty Harrison’s concert-length ‘Going / Places’. This long series of aural postcards, fractured and remoulded using the usual acousmatic devices, somehow failed to remind me of the experience of being in any place in particular, except perhaps in a hall surrounded by speakers at an acousmatic music concert. Barry Truax’s ‘Pendledrøm’, on the other hand, effectively conveyed the impression of a commute through Copenhagen, in which the weary commuter is half-aware of her familiar, routine surroundings and half drifting along in a dreamlike state. As I realised during Margetson’s piece, it’s primarily by means of harmony that sounds are linked to space, much as time and space are linked by way of memory. The fact that explicit harmony is by no means essential to the transportative effects of music suggests that the former is only a smoke that both announces and obscures some other fire. Alexander Pospischil, ‘Ichi-Kousatsu’ The installations at this year’s BEAST FEaST were fantastic. In John Kefala Kerr’s ‘Book of Bells’, the visitor was invited to locate passages from various antique books in order to complete a word search, ringing a different bell each time a passage is completed. In the background was a soundtrack featuring more bells and a cathedral choir. It was fun to do this task at the same time as other people, their bells ringing out at unexpected moments as I scanned yellow pages for sound references. Alexander Pospischil’s ‘Ichi-Kousatsu’ also required visitor participation, in the form of a chair positioned between a hanging tree branch and its shadow on the wall cast by the light from a projector. When I sat on the chair, branches began growing and budding out of my shadow, allowing me to experience, in a butoh-esque way, a sort of becoming-tree. The knocking together of branches in the wind in the installation’s audio component added to the overall effect. It was recently reported that scientists have discovered a discrete region of the brain that is activated when hearing music, and only when hearing music (not when hearing barking dogs, crackling fires, or any other sound). I wonder during how many pieces at BEAST FEaST the neurons in this part of my brain forgot to fire, or fired when they weren’t supposed to. Not everyone making work for sound systems such as BEAST thinks of what they do as ‘music’ in the traditional (neurological?) sense, but I found that the pieces that most engaged me, as a non-specialist member of the general public, were the ones that more clearly embraced musicality of some recognisable form or another. If the aim is to grow and broaden the horizons of this work in order to appeal to a wider audience and diversify its pool of practitioners, this may be one way to go. BEAST Cover image: BEAST tweeter arrays in the Elgar concert hall

items._cn_summary: BEAST FEaST 2016是一场以伯明翰大学多声道声场系统为核心的电子声学音乐盛会，评论聚焦于多首在空间声学与音色处理上各具特色的作品。Ben Peers以柔和低频嗡鸣营造沉静氛围，Emma Margetson的《Tick》将节拍器滴答声在时空中分裂折射，Annie Mahtani的《Aeolian》以雨后湿润质感转化日常田野录音，Helene Hedsund的《Bus No. 1》用低频振动模拟公交车地板并逐步瓦解为混沌。评论亦关注非传统手法：Tsun Winston Yeung将脑电波实时映射为声音，Kosmas Giannoutakis在钢琴与环绕算法间游走，Luca Danieli以机械化人声叙述服务器的孤独。整体评论强调多声道美学下的空间感、音色变形与舞台表演性，呈现电子声学创作的多样路径。

items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items.body: Review by Logan — The ambient, coolly nostalgic opening sequence of Geogaddi indicates the record's direction. Adjusting to the full album required some acclimation after years of listening to Music Has the Right to Children, but many elements appealed to me right away. Taking some distance from the debut allowed this strange, isolated world to make sense."Music Is Math" and "1969" rely on steady, ticking beats reminiscent of the D�sseldorf electronic scene, but with an uneasy feeling underneath. Further into the tracklist, pieces like "The Beach at Redpoint", "Gyroscope", and "Alpha and Omega" shift toward a darker Krautrock friction. The record relies on hypnotic, repetitive loops rather than traditional musical showmanship, focusing on old-sounding, distorted analog textures.My first favourite was clearly Music Has the Right to Children, which I found immediately accessible, followed by The Campfire Headphase, though I still loved Geogaddi during that era. However, it was only after Inferno came out that I deeply loved the final three albums, and the early material became more distant to me. This record is more like a 4.5 for me, though it gets a rounded-down 4 for Prog Archives purposes. Geogaddi is a strong exercise in sound design, but it remains a step below those late-career masterpieces for me. Inferno, The Campfire Headphase, and Tomorrow's Harvest mean the most to me these days, but all of Boards of Canada's albums I consider to be masterpieces in their own ways.Key tracks for me: "The Beach at Redpoint" and "Music is Math".
items._cn_summary: Boards of Canada 的第二张全长专辑延续了首作标志性的怀旧氛围与低科技模拟质感，但在情绪底色上转向更孤立、更不安。整张作品以催眠式循环和失真模拟纹理取代传统作曲逻辑，节拍参考杜塞尔多夫电子场景的稳定脉动，曲目中段则浮现德式摇滚式的摩擦感与暗流。多首作品不依赖旋律展开，而是通过采样碎片、变形的人声与老旧合成器音色构建一种疏离的声音空间。评论者指出该作需要脱离首作语境才能进入，自身最终给出约四星半的评价，肯定其在声音设计上的完成度，但认为它仍稍逊于乐队后期的几部作品。

items.body: Dreams may be among the strangest territories available to us. Each night, the mind constructs worlds without asking permission from physics, geography, biography, or common sense. We meet people who never existed, return to places that vanished years ago, fall in love with strangers, lose ourselves, recover ourselves, and wake carrying the emotional residue of events that never occurred. There is something almost miraculous in this private universe, because within it we are briefly released from the limits imposed by circumstance. Thought offers a similar freedom. We can imagine nearly anything, even when reality permits us to accomplish only a fraction of it. For Venus Volcanism, the Iceland-based project of Crete-born vocalist, musician, and producer Rena Rasouli, dreams become both refuge and research subject. Her new song, “Dreams,” inhabits the uncertain region between waking life and the private worlds that continue behind our eyes. Rasouli created the song exactly one year ago as the first snow settled across the peaks surrounding Siglufjörður, Iceland’s northernmost town. She keeps a journal beside her bed, recording complete dreams when possible and preserving stray images when that is all sleep leaves behind. Before sleeping, she gives herself a small invocation: “As I close my eyelids and sleep takes me, gently or not, please show me something that will help me understand myself a little better.” Dreams drifts somewhere between dark pop, ambient composition, experimental electronics, and neoclassical music, with affinities to This Mortal Coil, Julee Cruise, Penelope Trappes, and Zola Jesus. Rasouli’s voice occupies the center while drones, synthesizers, arpeggiated figures, and suspended textures create an unstable sense of location. Beauty and unease coexist. The song seems to hover between desire imagined and desire remembered. Its love story belongs to an imaginary lover, though imagination hardly makes the emotion less consequential. Desperation, longing, idealization, and obsession can become perfectly real experiences even when their object remains beyond reach. “Have you ever found yourself dreaming with your eyes open? I honestly don’t know how many times I have done it while diving into Icelandic pools,” says Rasouli. “Especially during winter, I feel like I am balancing somewhere between the conscious and the unconscious, and sometimes I don’t even know how the day has passed. I am and I am not. I exist and I do not exist. I do everything I am supposed to do; I move through the day as I should, but if you know me well enough, you might see it in my eyes: I am somewhere in between.” This suspended condition also governs the video, directed by Tassos Gkoletsos with help from friends and members of the Siglufjörður community. Northern Iceland’s long winter darkness turns ordinary routines into strange repetitions: tending plants, bathing, working, exercising, moving through familiar rooms while another existence unfolds internally. “During those months, I always find myself somewhere in between,” Rasouli continues. “I do everything I need to do and I’m relatively functional, but everything feels like autopilot. At the same time, another scene is taking place inside my head. I dream and imagine other things while going through the ordinary routines of everyday life, like watering my plants, having my bath, working, and going to the gym.” Perhaps this is why Dreams feels so intimate. Rasouli treats imagination as a parallel dimension of daily existence, one without measurable coordinates yet capable of altering everything that happens after we return. Watch the video for Dreams below: Listen to Dreams below and order the single here. items._cn_summary: 来自冰岛的希腊裔音乐人Rena Rasouli以梦境为创作核心，将暗黑流行、氛围、新古典与实验电子融为一体。作品诞生于冰岛最北小镇锡格吕菲厄泽的第一场雪中，人声居于中心，合成器持续音、琶音与悬置质感织就不稳定的空间感。歌曲叙述一段指向虚构爱人的情感，描摹欲望在想象与记忆之间的悬浮状态，与冰泉冬日的半意识状态形成互文。MV由当地社群共同参与完成，呈现日常生活在极夜中变形为陌生循环的影像。整体气质指向梦境与清醒的边界地带，音乐与歌词共同探讨自我理解的私人仪式。

items.body: Lift the veil, see what I’ve become An exoskeletal pantheon Born again from bone and breath To spread the living gospel of death On Tears for the Dying‘s blistering new gothic track Devour Me, Adria Stembridge drags the band back toward its earlier roots with a slower, heavier gait, then breaks that crawl apart with abrupt tempo changes that make the song feel unstable beneath your feet. Stembridge handles drum machine, guitar, bass, and vocals, building the track from dark guitar figures, blunt low-end pressure, and drums that move with the patience of something following you home. Her vocals hang above it all in a cold echo, less concerned with theatrical grandstanding than with letting the words rot in the air for a second before the next image lands. You can hear Bauhaus in the skeletal guitar work, Alien Sex Fiend in the queasy theatricality, and PiL and Fields of the Nephilim in the sense that somebody has wandered far enough from civilization to start inventing a religion. That religious impulse becomes central once the lyrics start opening the trapdoor. Stembridge draws from cosmic horror, but the terror here feels brutally physical. A solitary figure encounters an impossible swarm, loses control of the body piece by piece, and becomes host to something that treats flesh as raw material. Bones break. Insects burrow. The victim survives only in the technical sense, gradually becoming an alien deity whose transformation has erased whatever person existed before. The nastiest idea arrives afterward: worship. What begins as predation becomes conversion, and the ruined body becomes scripture. Consumption, reproduction, faith, and extermination collapse together until divinity itself starts looking like another parasitic infection. There is something wonderfully foul about that conception of godhood, especially coming from a band whose Southern gothic deathrock has long carried radical queer politics alongside its horror imagery. Authority here comes crawling out of meat. The slower passages give those images room to breathe before the faster sections shove everything toward panic. That contrast is crucial. Speed alone would turn the song into pursuit; the deliberate sections make you wait for whatever is chewing through the floorboards. By the final transformation, cosmic horror has lost every trace of abstraction. Infinity sprouts mandibles, theology breeds larvae, and salvation becomes a forced rebirth inside a body that has been converted into temple, nursery, and weapon. Listen to Devour Me below and order the single here. items._cn_summary: Tears for the Dying 新单曲以克苏鲁式的宇宙恐怖为叙事核心，将身体异变与宗教吞噬意象并置。Stembridge 一人操持鼓机、吉他、贝斯与人声，以慢速沉重的低频铺垫制造不安的爬行感，再以突然的节奏断裂打破张力。人声如冷回声漂浮于器乐之上，刻意收敛戏剧化铺张，让歌词的腐烂意象在空气中停滞。作品可辨识出 Bauhaus 的骨架式吉他、Alien Sex Fiend 的病态剧场感，以及 PiL 与 Fields of the Nephilim 远离文明后自创宗教的气质。南哥特死亡摇滚的传统中嵌入酷儿政治视角，使神权从肉体中爬出的意象具有额外锋利度。快慢段落交替构成恐惧的呼吸节奏，使最终的肉体转化为神殿、育婴所与武器三重合一时，宇宙恐怖彻底落地为生理层面的寄生虫感染。
